implementation_notes: net/http provides only composition: the enforcement point is the standard middleware idiom, a function that wraps an http.Handler, extracts credentials from the *http.Request, delegates verification to a verifier interface or a package such as an OIDC verifier, and either calls next.ServeHTTP or writes 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header. Wrap the mux once (http.ListenAndServe(addr, requireAuth(mux, verifier))) so the default is protected and public routes are explicitly unwrapped handlers; the interceptor class of the classic form is replaced by this function composition. The full structure is still justified when several transports share one policy, but for a single service the wrapped mux is the whole pattern.
pitfalls: The principal must travel in the request context (r.WithContext) or on the request itself; package-level variables are shared by concurrently served requests.
Wrapping individual routes instead of the mux makes the protected set implicit - any route registered later is public until someone remembers to wrap it.
